stem: Based on the text, what does it suggest about handwritten notes when they are used alone?
stimulus: For much of the twentieth century, linguists documented endangered languages mainly in handwritten notes. Notes record words well, but they often fail to capture tone, the rise and fall of pitch that changes a word's meaning in many languages. Today, most field linguists also make audio recordings, which preserve tone along with the words themselves.
choices: They cannot be used to record a language in any useful way.
They may leave out details needed to tell some words apart.
They preserve tone more reliably than audio recordings do.
They are no longer made by most linguists working in the field.
explanation: The text names one drawback of notes: they often miss tone, and tone changes what a word means. Go one step further and you get B: notes alone may lose the detail that tells one word from another. That is the whole move behind the real 'most strongly suggests' questions. Find the stated drawback of the old method, then say what it implies, and stop there.

A.why: You turned a limitation into a total failure. The text says notes 'record words well' and miss one thing, tone. It never says they are useless. This is the trap this question type is built around: the passage implies a weakness, and the wrong choice claims something absolute.

C.why: You reversed the contrast. The text says recordings preserve tone and notes often fail to. If you go back to the line, it says the opposite of this choice.

D.why: You read 'also make audio recordings' as 'make recordings instead'. 'Also' means linguists add recordings alongside their notes, so the text implies they still take notes.

stem: Based on the text, what does it suggest about self-healing concrete in places with cold winters?
stimulus: Self-healing concrete contains bacteria that produce limestone when water seeps into a crack, gradually sealing it. In laboratory trials, small cracks closed within a few weeks. However, the bacteria have been tested mostly at mild temperatures, and engineers do not yet know whether they survive repeated freezing. The material's promise in harsher climates therefore remains an open question.
choices: It has been shown to seal cracks through repeated freezing.
It will fail in any region where the temperature drops.
Its performance there has not yet been clearly established.
Its bacteria produce limestone when water enters a crack.
explanation: After 'However', the text says the bacteria were tested mostly at mild temperatures and nobody yet knows whether they survive freezing. The one-step inference is C: in cold places, we do not yet know how well it works. Hedges like 'do not yet know' and 'open question' set how sure your answer can be. On real inference questions, the correct choice matches that level of certainty.

A.why: You took the lab success and applied it to the case the text says was not tested. The passage says engineers do not know whether the bacteria survive freezing, so nothing has been shown.

B.why: You turned 'we don't know yet' into 'it fails'. This is this question type's trap: an untested limitation becomes an absolute claim. The text leaves the question open and does not predict failure.

D.why: The sentence is true, but it repeats how the material works and says nothing about cold winters. The question asks what the text implies about cold climates, so this choice does not do the job.

stem: Based on the example in the text, what does it suggest about the sugar figure printed on the cereal box?
stimulus: Nutrition labels can make a food look lighter than the way people actually eat it. For example, one cereal box lists its sugar content for a 30-gram serving. Yet when researchers asked adults to pour a normal breakfast, most filled their bowls with about 60 grams, twice the listed serving.
choices: It is likely to understate the sugar many adults actually eat.
It matches the amount most adults pour into a breakfast bowl.
It is reported in grams rather than in cups or spoonfuls.
It is deliberately false and should be removed from the box.
explanation: The label is based on 30 grams, and most adults poured 60. If people eat twice the serving, they take in more sugar than the label shows, so the figure understates their intake. The passage opens with a general claim and then gives one example to support it. Spotting that pattern helps on the real questions, because the inference usually connects the example back to the opening claim.

B.why: You missed the contrast set up by 'Yet'. Most adults poured about 60 grams, twice the 30-gram serving the label uses, so the label does not match what they pour.

C.why: You picked up an incidental detail, the unit. Grams appear in the passage, but the example is there to show a gap between the label and real portions, not to say anything about units.

D.why: You went two steps instead of one. The text says the figure is accurate for a smaller serving than people eat. It never says the label is false, intentional, or should be removed.

stem: Based on the text, what does it suggest about inspecting bridge cables by eye?
stimulus: Engineers once judged the condition of suspension-bridge cables mainly by eye, checking the surface for rust and broken wires. But corrosion often begins deep inside a cable, beneath layers of healthy-looking outer wire. Many agencies now attach acoustic sensors that detect the sharp sound of a single wire snapping within the bundle.
choices: It records the sound of wires snapping deep inside the bundle.
It never detects any damage at all on a suspension-bridge cable.
It finds hidden corrosion earlier than acoustic sensors can.
It can miss damage that has not yet reached the cable's surface.
explanation: 'But' brings in the real point: corrosion often starts inside the cable, under outer wire that looks healthy. An inspection that only looks at the surface can therefore miss that damage. That is D, exactly one step past the text. On harder inference questions, find the pivot word first. What comes after it is what the author wants you to conclude.

A.why: You gave visual inspection a feature that belongs to the new method. The acoustic sensors listen for snapping wires, and looking at a cable cannot hear anything.

B.why: You turned a blind spot into total failure. This is the trap this question type is built around. The text says inspectors checked for rust and broken wires on the surface, so looking does catch some damage. It just misses damage inside the cable.

C.why: You reversed the contrast. The text says corrosion hides under healthy-looking wire, which is why agencies added sensors. That implies looking finds hidden damage later, not earlier.
